summaries.information_need: Range based volatility estimation, grounded in extreme value theory, is weighed as an alternative to return based GARCH modeling for capturing dynamic volatility persistence, and the researcher wants to know what gap in the existing literature justifies developing a dedicated autoregressive framework for the range instead of adapting an existing conditional variance model.

A conditional autoregressive range model formulates the range's conditional mean autoregressively, in the manner of GARCH and the autoregressive conditional duration model, and the researcher wants to know whether this multiplicative error specification correctly enforces positivity while accommodating exogenous factors such as trading volume or lagged returns capturing leverage effects.

Quasi maximum likelihood estimation of a range based volatility model is applied under a possibly misspecified exponential density, and the researcher wants to know under what conditions this still yields consistent parameter estimates, how that guarantee is derived from the duration modeling framework, and what efficiency is sacrificed relative to a correctly specified alternative such as the Weibull distribution.

The autocorrelation function of a weekly price range series is compared against that of the absolute return series alongside distributional diagnostics, and the researcher wants to know whether the range shows markedly stronger serial dependence than returns, and whether summary statistics such as skewness and kurtosis justify committing to an explicit persistence model before estimation.

The leverage effect, the asymmetric response of volatility to lagged returns, is estimated within a range based conditional model, and the researcher wants to know whether its statistical significance exceeds what is typically found in return based GARCH models, and which diagnostic tests, such as a goodness of fit test on the residual distribution, validate the chosen lag order.

A Weibull distribution is considered as a replacement for the exponential error density in a range based volatility model, and the researcher wants to know whether it better captures the empirical residual distribution, particularly for small range observations, and whether the choice of error distribution materially changes the resulting in sample volatility forecasts.
summaries.answer_type: empirical distribution comparison / goodness of fit assessment

summaries.information_need: Out of sample forecast evaluation of two competing volatility models is conducted across several ex post volatility proxies, and the researcher wants to know which evaluation metric, such as root mean squared error or mean absolute error, and which rolling window forecasting scheme are appropriate given that some proxies measure variance while others measure standard deviation.

A Mincer-Zarnowitz regression tests the unbiasedness and relative predictive power of two competing volatility forecasts, and the researcher wants to know how standard errors should be adjusted for heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and parameter estimation error, such as via the Newey-West procedure, when comparing explanatory power across different volatility proxies.
summaries.answer_type: test procedure / regression based forecast evaluation

summaries.information_need: A forecast encompassing test includes both competing volatility forecasts as regressors, and the researcher wants to know whether one model's forecast subsumes the information content of the other, and under what conditions standard inference on the resulting test statistics remains valid when neither forecast fully encompasses the other.

Robust range estimation is considered to reduce a price range measure's sensitivity to outliers, and the researcher wants to know whether alternative statistics such as a quantile range address this, and what other generalizations, such as a multivariate extension or a drift adjusted range incorporating opening and closing prices, would broaden a univariate range based framework.
